theme: The cupbearer and baker; Pharaoh’s dreams; Joseph exalted
readingInstruction: Read Genesis 40:1-41:57. Joseph in prison interprets dreams for two of Pharaoh’s officials. Two years later, Pharaoh has dreams of his own, and Joseph is finally remembered. The seventeen-year-old slave is now a thirty-year-old vizier of Egypt.
settingTheScene: Joseph has been in prison for some time. Two of Pharaoh’s officials, the chief cupbearer and the chief baker, are imprisoned with him, and each has a strange dream. Joseph interprets both. The cupbearer is restored to his position; the baker is executed. Joseph asks the cupbearer to remember him, but he forgets, for two years. Then Pharaoh has dreams that none of his wise men can interpret, and the cupbearer finally remembers Joseph. Joseph stands before Pharaoh, interprets the dreams, and is elevated to second in command over all of Egypt.
observation: Joseph’s first words about dream interpretation: “Do not interpretations belong to God? Please tell them to me” (40:8).
Joseph correctly interprets both dreams, but the cupbearer forgets him.
Two years pass before Pharaoh’s dream. Joseph is in his early thirties when he finally stands before Pharaoh.
Pharaoh’s dreams: seven fat cows eaten by seven gaunt cows; seven good ears of grain eaten by seven blighted ears.
Joseph attributes everything to God: “It is not in me; God will give Pharaoh a favorable answer” (41:16).
He interprets the dream, seven years of plenty followed by seven years of famine, and recommends a plan.
Pharaoh promotes Joseph: “Can we find a man like this, in whom is the Spirit of God?”
Joseph receives Pharaoh’s signet ring, fine linen, a gold chain, and the second chariot. He is renamed Zaphenath-Paneah.
Joseph marries Asenath. They have two sons: Manasseh (“God has made me forget all my hardship”) and Ephraim (“God has made me fruitful in the land of my affliction”).
The seven years of plenty come and go; the famine arrives; people from every land come to Egypt to buy grain.
interpretation:
Genesis 40 and 41 are the turning point in Joseph’s story and the moment when the long providence of God becomes visible. For thirteen years, Joseph has been moving steadily downward, from favored son, to slave, to favored servant, to wrongly accused, to forgotten prisoner. In a single day, he ascends from prison to the second highest position in the empire.

The chapters teach us something essential about God’s timing. The cupbearer could have remembered Joseph immediately, and Joseph might have been freed. But God’s plan required Joseph in prison for two more years. Why? Because Pharaoh did not yet need a dream interpreter. The famine had not yet come. The whole reason God positioned Joseph in Pharaoh’s court was so that he could be there to manage the seven years of plenty and the seven years of famine. If Joseph had been released too early, he would have been just another freed slave. God’s timing requires the suffering.

Joseph’s interpretive principle is striking. “Do not interpretations belong to God?” he says in chapter 40. And to Pharaoh in chapter 41: “It is not in me; God will give Pharaoh a favorable answer.” Joseph has spent thirteen years in adversity. He has every reason to be bitter, to claim credit, to assert himself. Instead, he points to God at every turn. Notice that he is doing this before a pagan king who could grant him freedom or send him back to prison. Joseph is not editing his theology for a different audience. He says the same thing to Pharaoh that he said to the cupbearer in prison.

Pharaoh’s response is remarkable. “Can we find a man like this, in whom is the Spirit of God?” An Egyptian king recognizes the Spirit of God in a Hebrew slave. The same Spirit who will fill the prophets and ultimately fill Christ is at work in Joseph, and even Pharaoh can see it. The text is making a point: when God is genuinely with someone, even unbelievers can recognize it.

Joseph’s elevation is total. He receives Pharaoh’s signet ring (delegated authority), fine linen and a gold chain (royal insignia), and the second chariot (proximity to power). He is renamed, a sign of his new identity. He marries an Egyptian woman, Asenath. He has two sons whose names carry deep theological meaning. Manasseh, “God has made me forget all my hardship.” Joseph is naming his first son after the way God has worked in him. The bitter years are not erased, but they are now bearable. Ephraim, “God has made me fruitful in the land of my affliction.” Joseph is acknowledging that the place of his suffering became the place of his blessing. Egypt was the place of his slavery, his false accusation, his forgotten years. Now Egypt is the place of his fruitfulness. The land of affliction has become the soil of his calling.

Then the seven years of plenty come and go, and the famine arrives. The text says people from “all the earth” came to Egypt to buy grain. The stage is being set for the family of Jacob to make the journey south. Joseph is in place. The famine is the means. God is preparing to bring his promise, that Israel would sojourn in a land that was not theirs, into history.
connection: Joseph’s elevation is one of the great divine reversals in the Old Testament. Sold for twenty shekels of silver, he becomes the second most powerful man in Egypt. The reversal points forward to Christ, who, sold for thirty pieces of silver, became the King of kings. And the seven years of famine that will draw Joseph’s family to Egypt is the beginning of the four hundred years of sojourning that God predicted to Abram in Genesis 15.
application: Two truths to take with you. First, your timing is not God’s timing. The two years Joseph waited in prison felt unnecessary to him; they were essential to what God was doing. The waiting season you are in may feel pointless. It is not. God is using the time. Second, the place of your affliction may become the place of your fruitfulness. Egypt was Joseph’s land of suffering before it became the land of his calling. Whatever hard season you are in, physical, emotional, vocational, relational, God can make it the soil of unexpected fruit. Pray today that he will make you, like Joseph, fruitful in the land of your affliction.
prayerPrompts: Tell God about a season of waiting that feels pointless, and ask him to use it.
Ask him to make you fruitful where you are afflicted.
Ask for grace to give him credit in your conversations and work.
